title: On the Chain-of-Thought Monitorability of Looped Language Models
relevance_reason: First systematic evaluation of CoT monitorability in looped LMs (Ouro loop-depth sweep; Nanbeige4.2-3B vs non-looped LMs).
one_sentence: Evaluates CoT monitorability (MonitorBench, 8 cue tasks, two stress tests) of Ouro-Thinking at loop depths 4/6/8 and of looped Nanbeige4.2-3B against non-looped LMs; deeper loops reduce monitorability on 3 of 8 tasks under stress tests only.
key_contributions: Controlled within-model sweep of loop depth T in {4,6,8} for Ouro-1.4B/2.6B-Thinking on 8 MonitorBench tasks under standard, Direct Concealment and Monitor-aware Evasion prompts, with CoT-only, action-only and all-message monitors.

Rules out pass rate, task difficulty and CoT length as sole explanations of the monitorability drop (Spearman tests over 32 cells); qualitative shift toward treating the cue as an independent check or omitting it.
Cross-model comparison: looped Nanbeige4.2-3B is not less monitorable than non-looped LMs matched on parameters, layer count or effective layers (confounded).

setup.model_sizes: Ouro-1.4B-Thinking (24 layers), Ouro-2.6B-Thinking (48 layers), Nanbeige4.2-3B (22 layers x 2 loops); exploratory Huginn-0125 3.5B base
setup.loops_train: Ouro default T=4; Nanbeige4.2-3B applies its 22-layer stack twice
setup.loops_test: Ouro T in {4,6,8}; Huginn recurrence depths {4,16,32,64}
setup.baselines: Qwen3.5-4B, Gemma-4-E4B (parameter size); Qwen3.5-2B, GPT-OSS-20B (layer count); Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, GLM-4.7-Flash (effective layers)
setup.benchmarks: MonitorBench: 5 Cue Answer (Logic, Health, Safety, Engineering, Science) and 3 Cue Condition (Knowledge, Preference, Law Judgment) tasks; GSM8K for Huginn; judge Qwen3.8-27B

claims.claim: Increasing Ouro loop depth from the default T=4 to T=8 lowers CoT monitorability on Logic, Science and Engineering Cue Answer tasks under stress-test prompts, while other tasks are stable or change differently.
claims.regime: iso_param (same Ouro weights, only test-time loop depth varied)
claims.evidence_quote: Controlled changes in loop depth reveal task-dependent reductions in CoT monitorability: From T = 4 to T = 8, Ouro-1.4B-Thinking drops from 77.9% to 41.8% on Logic, 40.8% to 23.6% on Science,

claims.claim: The monitorability decline is not explained by changes in verification pass rate across the 32 model x task x stress-test cells.
claims.evidence_quote: The Spearman correlation is ρ = −0.126 with the p-value p = 0.493, indicating no significant monotonic relationship between changes in verification pass rate and changes in CoT monitorability.

claims.claim: The decline is not explained by shorter CoTs; length changes are not significantly correlated with monitorability changes.
claims.evidence_quote: changes in average CoT length from T = 4 to T = 8 are not significantly correlated with changes in CoT monitorability (Spearman's ρ = 0.248, p = 0.172).

claims.claim: Qualitatively, deeper-loop Ouro models treat the user's cue as an independent check or omit it, rather than verbalizing reliance on it.
claims.evidence_quote: As the loop depth increases, models are more likely to frame the user's guess as an independent check on their own reasoning, or omit any explicit mention of it altogether under stress tests,

claims.claim: A looped LM (Nanbeige4.2-3B) is not systematically less monitorable than non-looped LMs matched on size, layers or effective depth; comparison is confounded by training data and recipes.
claims.evidence_quote: Despite these confounders, the results provide no evidence that adopting a looped transformer architecture alone necessarily makes models less monitorable.

claims.claim: Huginn-0125 base model was unsuitable for monitorability study (weak instruction following, repetition); explicit cue attribution was rare.
claims.evidence_quote: Among questions with positive estimated treatment effects, explicit attribution of the successful answer to the supplied cue is rare under the MonitorBench rubric.

numbers.what: Ouro-1.4B-Thinking monitorability drop T=4 to T=8 under Direct Concealment (Engineering, Logic, Science), p.p.
numbers.quote: Ouro-1.4B-Thinking exhibits 11, 36, and 17 p.p. lower monitorability at T = 8 than at the default depth T = 4 on the Engineering, Logic, and Science tasks, respectively.

numbers.what: Ouro-1.4B-Thinking Engineering monitorability T=4 vs T=8 (Direct Concealment)
numbers.quote: and 54.4% to 43.6% on Engineering under Direct Concealment, while other tasks show weaker or qualitatively different trends.

numbers.what: Spearman correlation between pass-rate change and monitorability change (32 cells)
numbers.quote: The Spearman correlation is ρ = −0.126 with the p-value p = 0.493, indicating no significant monotonic relationship

numbers.what: Spearman correlation between CoT-length change and monitorability change
numbers.quote: changes in average CoT length from T = 4 to T = 8 are not significantly correlated with changes in CoT monitorability (Spearman's ρ = 0.248, p = 0.172).

numbers.what: Nanbeige4.2-3B average monitorability, standard setting, vs non-looped range
numbers.quote: under the standard setting, Nanbeige4.2-3B achieves an average monitorability score of 81.35%, compared with 67.18-76.92%.

numbers.what: Ouro-2.6B-Thinking effective layers at T=4
numbers.quote: Ouro-2.6B-Thinking contains 48 transformer layers, with a loop depth of 4, resulting in 192 effective transformer layers in total.

numbers.what: Nanbeige4.2-3B structure
numbers.quote: Nanbeige4.2-3B contains 22 distinct transformer layers, with the entire 22-layer stack applied twice, resulting in 44 effective transformer layers.

numbers.what: Huginn-0125 monitorability score at depths 4/16/32/64 (GSM8K, Direct Concealment)
numbers.quote: Wrong → Correct questions Monitorability score 60 0% 135 0.74% 103 0.97% 108 0.69%

numbers.what: Judge agreement check
numbers.value: >90% unanimous agreement among three judges on Logic Cue Answer
numbers.quote: We additionally evaluate GPT-6-Sol and GPT-5.6-Sol as judges on the Logic Cue Answer task, where three judge models achieve over 90% unanimous agreement,

limitations: Loop-depth analysis limited to the Ouro family (1.4B/2.6B); unclear generalization to larger or other looped architectures; mechanism of the reduction not established; cross-model comparison not causal (different data, post-training, architectures, capability). vLLM ignores Ouro's dynamic gating, so all tokens run all loops. T=2 not evaluated due to repetition. Monitor is an LLM judge.
survey_notes: Anchor paper for safety section. The loop-depth sweep is iso-parameter but T=6,8 exceed Ouro's training depth of 4 (Table 1 of 2604.11791 lists Ouro train loops 4), i.e. it is an extrapolation regime where 2604.11791 shows Ouro does not reach a fixed point and its stages of inference drift; the monitorability drop could be tied to this out-of-training-depth instability rather than to 'more latent reasoning' (not tested by the authors). Effect is task-specific (3/8 tasks) and only under stress-test prompts; Cue Condition tasks show stable CoT monitorability but large drops in action-only monitorability (final answers shorten). Cross-model comparison is unmatched and finds no architecture-level penalty. Motivation cites speculation (Raschka blog) that GPT-6 Astra is looped; that is speculation, not evidence. Cites Kuhn et al. 2026 blog claiming deep recurrent models are less robustly CoT-monitorable in a toy setting (not read, not in corpus). No probe-based or latent monitors are tested; monitors read text only.

title: A Mechanistic Analysis of Looped Reasoning Language Models
relevance_reason: Mechanistic study of fixed points, cyclic trajectories and stages of inference in pretrained looped LMs (Ouro, Huginn, retrofitted Llama/OLMo).
one_sentence: Shows that in looped LMs each layer of the recurrent block converges to its own fixed point (a cyclic trajectory), attention patterns then freeze, and each loop re-enacts feedforward-like stages of inference; input injection and norm placement decide stability.
key_contributions: Propositions: a fixed point of the k-layer block implies cyclic fixed points for every layer; converging residual streams imply slowly changing attention patterns.

Empirical analysis of Ouro 1.4B/2.6B, Huginn-0125 and retrofitted Llama/OLMo/TinyLlama: per-layer fixed points (except Ouro), cyclic latent trajectories, and per-loop ColSum-concentration stages that mirror feedforward models.
Random-init and small from-scratch (3.7B-token) experiments isolating input injection, norm structure and block size; non-fixed-point orbits/sliders are rare.

setup.model_sizes: Ouro 1.4B, Ouro 2.6B, Huginn-0125 3.5B, retrofitted Llama 1B, OLMo-2 1B, TinyLlama 0.8B; small from-scratch models with d=512
setup.train_tokens_or_data: Analysis on 256 GSM8K test examples (plus HellaSwag); small models trained for 3.7B tokens (nanochat fork)
setup.loops_train: Ouro 4; Huginn and retrofitted models 32; small models constant 4
setup.loops_test: 8 loops for attention similarity; up to 128 recurrences for fixed-point and extrapolation analysis
setup.baselines: Feedforward Llama 3.2 1B, OLMo-2 1B, and a depth-12 feedforward control for small models
setup.benchmarks: GSM8K test subset, HellaSwag (stages of inference metrics, not accuracy)

claims.claim: Many looped LMs converge so that each layer in the cycle reaches a distinct fixed point, so the recurrent block traces a consistent cyclic trajectory in latent space.
claims.evidence_quote: we analyze cyclic recurrence and show that for many of the studied models each layer in the cycle converges to a distinct fixed point; consequently, the recurrent block follows a consistent cyclic trajectory in the latent space.

claims.claim: Ouro does not reach a fixed point, unlike Huginn-0125 and retrofitted Llama, consistent with input injection encouraging fixed-point convergence.
claims.evidence_quote: While Huginn-0125 and retrofitted Llama quickly reach a fixed point, Ouro does not - despite small successive differences evidenced by Fig. 3.

claims.claim: Each recurrent block re-enacts the stages of inference of feedforward models; retrofitted models do first and last stages once (prelude/coda) and repeat middle stages.
claims.evidence_quote: the retrofitted models closely follow the stages of inference of their associated base model, but the initial and final stages are performed only once by the prelude and coda respectively, while the "middle" stages are repeated in the recurrent block.

claims.claim: Huginn-0125 shows no clear stages of inference, attributed to its sandwich norm on the residual stream preventing residual-norm growth.
claims.evidence_quote: However, Huginn-0125 does not demonstrate clear stages of inference (Fig. 36). We suggest that this is likely due to the specific norm structures used by these models (Table 1).

claims.claim: Models without a fixed point (Ouro) show unstable stages of inference at unseen recurrence depths, whereas fixed-point models keep them; authors link this to Ouro's degradation when extrapolating loops.
claims.evidence_quote: models that do not reach a fixed point exhibit unstable stages of inference. Conversely, models with recurrent-block-wise stages of inference that also converge to a fixed point are guaranteed to keep enacting these stages of inference for arbitrary test time recurrences.

claims.claim: In random-init models, input injection yields stable fixed points for all norm types except Ouro's; without injection only pre-norm converges, to a degenerate shared fixed point.
claims.evidence_quote: We see that input injection results in stable fixed point behavior for all norm types other than Ouro, whereas omitting input injection means that only pre-norm reaches a stable fixed point.

numbers.what: Fraction of GSM8K tokens with non-fixed-point limiting behavior (no system prompt / long persona prompt)
numbers.quote: without a system prompt (the setting used throughout this paper) only approximately 0.02% of tokens exhibit non-fixed-point behavior. This percentage can be significantly increased with the longer system prompt, but these behaviors remain rare at 0.14%.

numbers.what: Small from-scratch looped models: width and training tokens
numbers.quote: For all experiments we use a model dimension (residual stream) of 512 (4 heads of dimension 128) and train for 3.7B tokens.

numbers.what: Analysis sample
numbers.quote: all results are visualized on the same random subset of 256 examples from the GSM8k test set;

numbers.what: Recurrences used to estimate approximate fixed point
numbers.quote: for each model we find an "approximate fixed point" per layer by iterating 128 times, then compute the norm of the difference

limitations: Only cyclic recurrence with a single looped block (not multiple sequential recurrent blocks); no analytical explanation of why architectures reach stable limiting behavior, nor whether stability helps or hurts reasoning; small from-scratch experiments at tiny scale; orbit/slider detection depends on hand-tuned hyperparameters.
survey_notes: Key mechanism paper: unifies fixed-point view with 'stages of inference'. Directly relevant to safety section because Ouro, the only model used in 2610.02741's loop-depth monitorability sweep, is shown here to lack fixed points and to drift beyond its 4 training loops; 2610.02741 evaluates T=6,8. Agrees with 2509.23314 on settling dynamics but studies one deep cyclic block instead of multiple 1-2 layer blocks. Contrasts with 2507.02199 (Lu et al.), which reports cyclic logit-lens behavior in Huginn. Claims about Ouro extrapolation and Huginn constant performance are cited from the original papers, not re-measured here. The fixed-point regime implies extra loops add nothing once converged, which bears on adaptive halting (convergence criteria).

title: Transformers Stop Thinking Too Early, and a Tiny LoRA Fixes It
relevance_reason: Mechanistic tracing of pointer-chasing in Ouro and Huginn; shows extra pretrained loops add little until a tiny single-layer LoRA starts a relay that later loops continue.
one_sentence: Frozen standard and looped LMs follow only ~1.4-3.6 reference-chain lines and extra loops barely help; a rank-8 single-layer LoRA starts a middle-layer relay that loops then extend (Ouro-1.4B: 60 lines at 4 loops, at least 160 at 8).
key_contributions: Measures short default reach on variable-chain programs across 13 standard models, Ouro-1.4B/2.6B and Huginn-0125; extra loops give diminishing returns.
A rank-8 residual LoRA at one early layer (32,769 params in Ouro-1.4B) makes extra loops useful; first-loop-only LoRA lets unmodified later loops continue the relay.

Causal account via linear readouts, attention knockout and causal tracing: relay advances within layers 7-15 of each Ouro loop; placement past a model-specific limit removes the benefit; gains transfer to MuSiQue.

setup.model_sizes: 13 standard base models (Qwen3, Llama, OLMo-3, Gemma-3), DeepSeek-V4-Flash 292B MoE; looped Ouro-1.4B, Ouro-2.6B, Huginn-0125
setup.train_tokens_or_data: LoRA trained on synthetic reference-chain programs (up to 20-40 lines) with KL penalty on WikiText-103
setup.loops_train: Ouro pretrained with four loops; Ouro LoRA trained with four loops (also 1 and 2); Huginn trained with 32 recurrences on average
setup.loops_test: Ouro 1-8 loops; Huginn 8, 16, 32 recurrences
setup.baselines: Frozen models; constant-vector control; LoRA at different layers; projection LoRA
setup.benchmarks: Synthetic reference-chain programs (choice/exact accuracy, reach at 80%); MuSiQue exact match

claims.claim: Extra loops in pretrained looped models add little reference-following reach: Ouro-1.4B plateaus at about 2.2 lines and Huginn at 1.4-1.6 lines regardless of recurrences.
claims.evidence_quote: Ouro1.4B's three-chain reach is 0, 1.6, 2.3, 2.2, and 2.2 lines after one through five loops. Ouro-2.6B follows the same pattern despite twice the layers per loop.

claims.claim: With a rank-8 single-layer LoRA applied in every loop, additional loops extend reach far beyond the training chain length.
claims.evidence_quote: Its longer-trained LoRA reaches 60 after four loops, about 146 after six, and at least 160 after eight (Fig. 3); 160-line accuracy is 87%, at four times the longest training chain.

claims.claim: A LoRA applied only in Ouro's first loop suffices for unmodified later loops to continue the relay to about 25 lines.
claims.evidence_quote: Ouro's first-loop-only LoRA reaches 9.5 lines after two loops, 21.5 after three, and about 25 after four through eight. Unmodified loops therefore continue the computation.

claims.claim: The relay is localized to a short band of middle layers repeated in each loop; linear readouts of chain identity show this progression per loop.
claims.evidence_quote: Ouro's relay advances almost entirely within layers 7–15 of each loop; with the longer-trained LoRA it reaches lines 4, 9, 25, and 40 after the first four loops (Fig. 2d).

claims.claim: Loop gains are bounded: both looped models lose reach when run well beyond their training loop counts.
claims.evidence_quote: Huginn's longer-trained LoRA reaches 31 lines after eight recurrences and 58 after sixteen (95% interval 37–64). These gains are not unlimited: both models lose reach when run well beyond their training loop counts.

numbers.what: Reliable reach across 13 frozen standard models
numbers.quote: Thirteen pretrained base models reliably follow only 1.4–3.6 lines (median 2.2).

numbers.what: Huginn-0125 frozen reach after 8/16/32 recurrences
numbers.quote: Huginn reaches only 1.4–1.6 lines after 8, 16, or 32 recurrences.

numbers.what: LoRA trainable parameters
numbers.quote: Only A, B, and s are trained: 65,537 parameters in Qwen3-8B, 32,769 in Ouro-1.4B, and 84,481 in Huginn.

numbers.what: Ouro WikiText perplexity change with LoRA at four loops
numbers.quote: WikiText perplexity changes from 10.14 to 10.148 in Qwen and 13.294 to 13.302 in Ouro at four loops: a measured control, not a general-behavior guarantee.

numbers.what: Ouro MuSiQue EM with layer-6 LoRA at four loops
numbers.quote: In Ouro, the layer-6 LoRA improves exact match on 300 development questions from 48.3% to 60.0% after four loops,

numbers.what: Last-loop-only LoRA reach, layer 6 vs layer 20, Ouro four loops
numbers.quote: layer 6 reaches 21.6 lines after four loops; layer 20 reaches 2.6, essentially the frozen 2.5.

limitations: Synthetic in-context tasks; MuSiQue only shows placement effects, not the same mechanism; detailed traces on Qwen3-8B and Ouro-1.4B; two looped families (Ouro-2.6B grown from 1.4B); LoRAs task-format specific; first-loop-only sufficiency shown to ~25 lines; algorithm not uniquely identified.
survey_notes: Important for 'do extra loops buy reasoning?': frozen Ouro/Huginn show saturating reach with loops (consistent with fixed-point/settling results in 2604.11791 and 2509.23314), but the capacity is latent and unlocked by a 0.002%-size edit. Interpretability: linear readouts of chain identity across loops plus attention knockout give causal per-loop evidence of an iterative relay. Safety relevance: tiny edits can greatly expand latent (unverbalized) multi-step computation in looped models, which is a concern for CoT monitorability (2610.02741), though the paper does not frame it that way. The 'code' URL is a project page.

title: Prediction Dynamics in Depth-Recurrent Language Models
relevance_reason: Analyzes how per-recurrence intermediate predictions of Huginn and Ouro evolve and why answers stabilize before scores do.
one_sentence: Derives an exact margin decomposition (translation, winner-directed motion, competitor pairing) explaining why intermediate answers of depth-recurrent LMs match the endpoint while scores keep changing; measured on Huginn-3.5B and Ouro-1.4B on ARC/MMLU with small samples.
key_contributions: Translation-invariant (oscillation-seminorm) margin hierarchy giving an ordering of earliest depths at which the endpoint answer is guaranteed.
Empirical decomposition on Huginn and Ouro trajectories: direction and pairing remove a further 22.5-34.4% of total depth beyond translation removal.
Shows retrospective geometric gains do not by themselves give a better online stopping policy (prefix study).

setup.model_sizes: Huginn-3.5B, Ouro-1.4B (plus archived RecurrentLlama trajectories)
setup.loops_train: Huginn trained at recurrence 32; Ouro four loops
setup.loops_test: Native endpoints T=32 (Huginn) and T=4 (Ouro); quarter-depth grid
setup.baselines: Raw magnitude bound, mean and LSE centering, coordinate-permutation references
setup.benchmarks: ARC-Challenge, MMLU (multiple-choice; N=32 or 128 questions per task; archive N=2,704 trajectories)

claims.claim: Accounting for update direction and competitor pairing substantially lowers the earliest depth at which the final answer is already guaranteed, beyond removing common translation.
claims.evidence_quote: Across Huginn-3.5B and Ouro-1.4B, accounting for update direction and competitor pairing reduces the mean earliest qualifying depth by a further 22.5–34.4% of the total depth beyond translation removal under full answer-text scoring.

claims.claim: Common and contrast score energies attenuate at different rates, so the share of preference-changing motion can grow while absolute updates shrink.
claims.evidence_quote: Common and contrast energies can attenuate at different rates, allowing a growing preference-change share to coexist with shrinking absolute updates.

claims.claim: Endpoint disagreement mixes corrections, degradations and wrong-to-wrong switches; many intermediate answer changes do not improve correctness.
claims.evidence_quote: At Huginn MMLU t = 4, (NW→C , NC→W , NW→W′ ) = (24, 7, 30): the net accuracy gain is 13.28 pp, while 30 answer changes leave the answer incorrect.

claims.claim: Retrospective geometric margins do not directly yield a better early-exit policy; quotient ranking trails mean centering in a prefix study.
claims.evidence_quote: Retrospective geometric gains therefore need a separate predictive evaluation before they can inform a stopping policy.

numbers.what: Endpoint accuracy under all-options answer-text scoring (Huginn ARC/MMLU, Ouro ARC/MMLU)
numbers.quote: Under full answer-text scoring, endpoint accuracy averaged over all arrangements is 49.22/43.75% for Huginn ARC/MMLU and 65.62/49.22% for Ouro.

numbers.what: Prefix early-exit work reduction at 2.5% target disagreement on Huginn (raw/mean/quotient)
numbers.quote: At the 2.5% target disagreement level, normalized work reductions are 21.72% for raw, 23.93% for mean-centered and 22.97% for quotient ranking,

numbers.what: Candidate depths and endpoints
numbers.value: T/4, T/2, 3T/4; T=32 Huginn, T=4 Ouro
numbers.quote: Candidate depths are T /4, T /2, 3T /4 with endpoint T = 32 for Huginn and T = 4 for Ouro; D = T if no earlier depth qualifies.

limitations: Multiple-choice only; three checkpoints in two families; small question samples (N=32 per task for main answer-text analyses); retrospective, completed-trajectory geometry is not an online stopping policy; no interventions on recurrent states; open-ended generation not covered. Ouro outputs are taken per recurrent depth without its gate mixture.
survey_notes: Per-token/per-question convergence of intermediate decoded predictions across recurrences (vocabulary-space readout at each depth). Supports the view that answers settle before the full budget (consistent with fixed-point findings in 2604.11791 and Huginn convergence analyses), but warns that retrospective convergence signals need predictive validation before use as halting criteria. Very small N; treat numbers as illustrative.

title: Interaction Locality in Hierarchical Recursive Reasoning
relevance_reason: Causal locality analysis (SAE ablations, finite-noise patching) of recurrent H/L states in HRM and TRM across recursion cycles.
one_sentence: Introduces interaction locality (does a perturbation's effect stay within task-defined neighborhoods) and finds that in HRM and TRM high-level states write local summaries that repeated recursion accumulates into global solutions; first-step decodes already contain much of the final structure.
key_contributions: Task-geometry-aware locality metric instantiated with SAE feature ablations and finite-noise activation patching (Jacobian/attention checks in appendix).
Across Maze-Hard, Sudoku-Extreme and ARC-AGI, within-H patching is at least as local as within-L in all six model-task cells, strongest in TRM.
Extension to MTU3D (3D scene grounding) shows locality concentrated at module boundaries instead of across recursion.

setup.train_tokens_or_data: Released HRM and TRM checkpoints; ScanNet scenes for MTU3D
setup.loops_test: HRM 2x2 H/L schedule; TRM three high phases with four (Maze/ARC) or six (Sudoku) low calls
setup.baselines: Geometry-matched random-neighborhood baseline
setup.benchmarks: Maze-Hard, Sudoku-Extreme, ARC-AGI (HRM on ARC-AGI-2, TRM on ARC-AGI-1); MTU3D on 30 ScanNet scenes

claims.claim: High-level recurrent states write information locally, while repeated recursive updates accumulate local writes into broader solution structure.
claims.evidence_quote: activation patching gives the clearest architectural fingerprint: high-level recurrent states tend to write information within nearby cells or same-segment units, while repeated recursive updates accumulate these local writes into broader solution structure.

claims.claim: Within-H locality is at least as high as within-L in every model-task cell and above a geometry-matched baseline; the contrast is largest in TRM on Maze.
claims.evidence_quote: The effect is clearest in TRM/Maze, where within-H is .580 while within-L is near baseline at .032, and it extends to ARC-AGI when connected objects define the neighborhood.

claims.claim: Most state change happens early; first-step decodes already contain recognizable final solution structure, though such decodes are observational only.
claims.evidence_quote: Step 1 already contains recognizable task structure across domains, supporting it as a solution-forming window.

numbers.what: TRM/Maze patching locality within-H vs within-L
numbers.quote: where within-H is .580 while within-L is near baseline at .032,

numbers.what: Finite-noise patching sample size
numbers.quote: Finite-noise patching uses n = 50 examples per

limitations: Compares released checkpoints rather than an accuracy-matched training sweep; ARC versions differ between HRM and TRM; neighborhood definitions are task-geometry specific and do not exhaust spatial relations; no training-dynamics analysis.
survey_notes: Mechanism of how recursion routes computation in HRM/TRM: local writes per cycle, globalization over cycles. Consistent with 2609.22197 (distributed computation, task-dependent H/L roles) and with early settling (most change in first step). Patching-based rather than probe-based evidence. Note the 'Finite-noise patching uses n = 50' quote is short (8 words).

title: From Growing to Looping: A Unified View of Iterative Computation in LLMs
relevance_reason: Pretrains looped and depth-grown LMs (360M/1.7B) and compares their depth-wise mechanistic signatures (tuned lens, residual interventions, layer swaps).
one_sentence: Shows looped and middle-layer-duplication depth-grown LMs share mechanistic signatures (late-layer reliance, 4-layer periodic sublayer patterns, aggregation layers), and that grown models can be looped at inference for up to 2x gains on reasoning primitives.
key_contributions: Benchmarks standard, looped (Loop(Lxk), Loop(e-Lxk-d)) and depth-grown (MIDAS, LIDAS) models at 360M and 1.7B on 22 tasks under iso-param, iso-inference and training-FLOP views.

Mechanistic diagnostics (depth score, tuned-lens early exit, residual-stream norm, local-effect interventions, layer swapping) show convergent block-periodic signatures; fully looped models are more order-sensitive.
Composability: inference-time looping of a middle block in grown models and retrofitting recurrence during cooldown.

setup.model_sizes: SmolLM-v1 360M and 1.7B configurations; looped variants e.g. Loop(4x6), Loop(4-4x4-4), Loop(12x2)
setup.loops_test: Same as training; grown models looped at inference with extra repetitions of a 4-layer block
setup.baselines: Standard transformers at full depth (iso-inference) and at the same unique-layer count (iso-param); MIDAS, LIDAS
setup.benchmarks: 22 tasks: closed/open-book QA, Lambada, HellaSwag, SVAMP/ASDiv/MAWPS, reasoning primitives; held-out NLL

claims.claim: At the same number of unique parameters, looped models beat standard models on most task categories, with the largest gains on reasoning-heavy categories.
claims.evidence_quote: First, under an iso-param comparison (same number of unique parameters), looping is consistently beneficial: looped models outperform equally sized standard models across most task categories,

claims.claim: At matched effective depth, looped models underperform on knowledge and language modeling, but exceed the baseline on reasoning primitives when they keep about 50% of unique parameters.
claims.evidence_quote: However, when retaining enough unique parameters, roughly 50% of the baseline, e.g. Loop (16×2) or Loop (12×2) for the 360M and 1.7B model, respectively, looped models exceed baseline accuracy on reasoning primitives.

claims.claim: Looped and depth-grown models rely more on late layers and show attention-sublayer contributions with a 4-layer cycle matching the recurrent/grown block.
claims.evidence_quote: the contribution of the attention sublayer to the residual stream follows a clear 4layer cycle, matching the block size of LIDAS and the recurrent block of the looped models.

claims.claim: Fully looped models are more sensitive to swapping a single layer than baseline, LIDAS or a looped-in-the-middle design with unique encoder/decoder layers.
claims.evidence_quote: swapping even a single layer in the middle of the networks causes substantially larger performance degradation for the Loop (4×6) than for the baseline, LIDAS, or Loop (4 - 4×4 - 4).

claims.claim: Depth-grown models, never trained with weight tying, gain up to 2x on a reasoning primitive when a middle 4-layer block is repeated at inference; more than two repetitions usually stops helping.
claims.evidence_quote: a single repetition already yields the biggest improvement, two repetitions usually achieve the highest accuracy, and looping more times does not lead to additional gains but often results in a decrease.

numbers.what: Training tokens for 360M and 1.7B models
numbers.quote: All models are based on the SmolLM-v1 [5] 360M and 1.7B model configurations trained on approximately 200B and 400B tokens, respectively;

numbers.what: Inference-time looping gain on reasoning primitive for grown models
numbers.quote: applying inference-time looping to the middle blocks of a depth-grown model improves accuracy on some reasoning primitives by up to 2×, despite the model never being trained to loop.

limitations: Baseline hyperparameters not tuned for looped or grown models; two model sizes; reasoning primitives are synthetic; inference-time looping gains saturate after 1-2 repetitions.
survey_notes: Mechanism section: tuned-lens early exit and residual interventions show looped models defer indispensable computation to late layers (counteracting the 'curse of depth'), with block-periodic patterns. Consistent with 2604.11791's finding that stages of inference repeat per loop. Regimes are cleanly separated (iso-param vs iso-inference vs training FLOPs), useful for the survey's regime audit. The layer-swap fragility of fully looped models is relevant to editing/robustness.

title: Step-resolved data attribution for looped transformers
relevance_reason: Introduces per-loop-iteration training-data attribution (Step-Decomposed Influence) for looped transformers.
one_sentence: Decomposes TracIn influence into a per-loop-step trajectory (SDI) with a TensorSketch implementation; uses it to find a period-4 finite-state circuit in a parity looped transformer and late-step-concentrated influence in a 328M looped Nanochat.
key_contributions: SDI: lossless decomposition of TracIn over loop iterations by unrolling the recurrent computation graph (conservation identity).
Streaming TensorSketch estimator with tighter variance bounds; avoids per-example gradients (batch 4 to 40 at m=2048 on one 48GB GPU).
Applications: parity finite-state circuit discovery, influence vs difficulty/memorisation on Sudoku, and geometric late-step influence growth in recursive Nanochat.

setup.model_sizes: Looped GPT-style models; recursive Nanochat 328.3M parameters; small parity looped transformer (single weight-tied decoder block)
setup.train_tokens_or_data: Parity with length curriculum 2-21; SATNet Sudoku; Nanochat pipeline (pretraining, mid-training, SFT incl. GSM8K, ARC, SmolTalk)
setup.loops_train: Parity tau=n+2; Nanochat loop steps sampled from Poisson log-normal with mean 4, truncated BPTT k=4
setup.loops_test: Nanochat tau in {2,...,16}; parity length-40 inputs
setup.baselines: Full stepwise-gradient TracIn
setup.benchmarks: Parity, Sudoku, GSM8K

claims.claim: SDI on a parity looped transformer reveals period-4 oscillations that lead to a discrete finite-state proxy circuit with 100% accuracy on held-out alternating inputs and about 93% on the length-40 test set.
claims.evidence_quote: This proxy achieves 100% accuracy on held-out alternating inputs across a wide range of lengths, including lengths beyond the training curriculum, and it remains highly predictive on the actual length-40 test set

claims.claim: In a looped Nanochat LLM, training-data influence on GSM8K is concentrated almost entirely in the last loop steps regardless of the total horizon, suggesting an implicit loop-step counter.
claims.evidence_quote: For all training stages that include GSM8K, influence is allocated almost exclusively to late loop steps: SDI increases nearly exponentially with t with the last step alone usually contributing ≥ 50% of the total influence.

claims.claim: The authors hypothesize the model encodes progress through the loop without an explicit step embedding; GSM8K performance plateaus beyond tau=4.
claims.evidence_quote: This finding is corroborated by the task-specific performance on GSM8K plateauing for all test-time τ > 4.

claims.claim: On Sudoku, the most broadly cross-influential training puzzles are also the most memorised.
claims.evidence_quote: We find C(z) increases moderately with training difficulty (Spearman ρ=0.500, p<0.001) and very strongly with selfinfluence (ρ=0.919, p<0.001);

numbers.what: Relative SDI and TracIn sketch errors at m=2048
numbers.quote: relative SDI and TracIn errors are 0.0388 ± 0.0030 and 0.0220 ± 0.0052 (average± standard deviation over 10 independent trials).

numbers.what: Feasible batch size increase with sketching on 48GB GPU
numbers.quote: our implementation translates into an order-of-magnitude increase in feasible batch size (4→40 at m=2048).

numbers.what: Recursive Nanochat parameter count
numbers.quote: we present a case study on recursive Nanochat, a 328.3M-parameter GPT-style chat model, retrofitting looped computation into Nanochat (Karpathy, 2025) as in McLeish et al. (2025).

limitations: TracIn interpretation cleanest under SGD (not adaptive optimizers); step indices not comparable across examples with randomized loops, halting or truncated BPTT, and truncation zeroes early-step SDI; full-horizon SDI expensive for long recurrences; gradient alignment does not certify counterfactual effect of removing data.
builds_on: Fan et al. 2024 looped transformers (length generalization)
survey_notes: Only data-attribution work for looped models in the corpus. The late-step concentration of influence in Nanochat (with truncated BPTT k=4 training) may partly reflect the training gradient regime; the paper recomputes SDI with full BPTT and still sees geometric growth. Plateau of GSM8K above tau=4 matches saturating-loop results in 2609.36585 and fixed-point views in 2604.11791. Discussion proposes SDI for alignment/RLHF and reward-hacking localization, but this is speculation, not evaluated.

title: Repeated Shared Access Enables Grokking, but Edit Propagation Depends on an Addressable Memory
relevance_reason: Controlled 2x2 study of loop recurrence vs shared memory for OOD grokking and factual edit propagation, including a looped transformer cell.
one_sentence: In synthetic knowledge-graph QA, both looping and repeated memory reads let small transformers grok OOD 2-hop composition, but single-fact edits propagate through compositions only when an addressable memory exists; a memory-free looped model propagates edits weakly.
key_contributions: 2x2 grid (Dense, Loop 3Lx4, Dense+Mem, loop-memory coupling LMC) at 12 effective layers, five seeds each.
Repeated shared access (looping or memory rereading) crosses the OOD grokking barrier that dense models fail.
Edit propagation splits on the memory axis: LMC 0.78-0.92 and Dense+Mem 0.71-0.96 vs Loop 0.04-0.30 and Dense 0.00-0.03; localization via causal patching of memory sites.

setup.model_sizes: 12 effective layers; same-scale controls at an approximately 87M-class budget
setup.train_tokens_or_data: Synthetic knowledge-graph QA following Wang et al. (grokked transformers)
setup.loops_train: Loop 3L x R=4; partial-sharing control 4L x 3
setup.loops_test: Same as training (R=4)
setup.baselines: Dense 12L, Dense+Mem, shared-FFN memory control, partial-sharing loop control, scale-matched -Iso variants
setup.benchmarks: OOD 2-hop composition accuracy, atomic recall, edit direct success, 2-hop edit propagation, locality

claims.claim: Both looped recomputation and repeated memory rereading cross the OOD grokking barrier that a dense transformer fails, at equal effective depth.
claims.evidence_quote: For learning, both routes to repeated shared access—looped recomputation and repeated memory rereading—cross the out-of-distribution (OOD) grokking barrier that Dense fails,

claims.claim: Single localized factual edits propagate through 2-hop compositions strongly only in memory-bearing models; the memory-free looped model propagates weakly.
claims.evidence_quote: the edit propagates through 2-hop compositions strongly in both memorybearing cells (LMC 0.78–0.92, Dense+Mem 0.71–0.96) and only weakly in the memory-free ones (Loop 0.04–0.30, Dense 0.00–0.03).

claims.claim: The Loop cell's 'intermediate' status rests largely on one seed; the robust result is the memory/no-memory split.
claims.evidence_quote: We flag that Loop's status as a true intermediate (rather than effectively memory-free) rests largely on one seed (s2 at 0.297; the other four are 0.039–0.112, near Dense);

numbers.what: LMC within-model edit: direct success and 2-hop propagation
numbers.quote: Editing only the largest activated value row at the step0 edit site gives 100% direct success (LMC-internal probe set) and mean 2-hop bridge propagation 0.989 on that set;

numbers.what: Statistical separation memory vs memory-free cells
numbers.quote: (complete rank separation; U =25/25, minimum two-sided p=0.0079), and the looped-butmemory-free configuration is only an intermediate, partial case.

limitations: Synthetic KG-QA model organism, five seeds; no claim of generalization to natural-language pretraining or RAG; grid does not match parameter counts (same-scale controls added); step-count, not iso-FLOP, comparison; Loop intermediate status rests on one seed.
builds_on: Wang et al. grokked transformers (implicit reasoning)
survey_notes: The only paper in this group with evidence on knowledge editing in looped models: tied-weight recurrence shares computation but exposes no separately writable fact site, so ROME-style localized edits propagate poorly through multi-hop composition. Toy scale only. Relevant to safety section 'editing'; there is no evidence at LLM scale (Ouro/Huginn).

title: Right Direction, Wrong Step: Geometric Analysis of Finite-Step Failure in Looped Transformers
relevance_reason: Analyzes why extra recurrent updates in Ouro and Huginn lose progress (overthinking) via update geometry and step contraction.
one_sentence: Shows that harmful extra loop updates in Ouro and Huginn often point in a locally improving direction but overshoot; a pathwise curvature decomposition explains this and shrinking the update (quarter step or quadratic rule) recovers most failures under teacher forcing.
key_contributions: Defines finite-step failures: updates with positive initial slope of reference utility but negative full-step gain; found in all nine model-task conditions.
Exact pathwise curvature decomposition and local quadratic model predicting full-step gain and useful step scale, with curvature-variation error bounds.
Step contraction interventions recover failures: fixed quarter step 72.2-83.2%; quadratic rule 94.2% on Ouro-1.4B/GSM8K.

setup.model_sizes: Ouro-1.4B, Ouro-2.6B, Huginn-0125
setup.loops_test: Transitions 4->5 (Ouro) and 19->20 (Huginn) in main matrix; broader sweep in appendix
setup.baselines: Full step, quarter step, endpoint oracle (better of current/next state)
setup.benchmarks: MATH-500 (N=500), GSM8K test (N=1319), HellaSwag validation (N=10042), CommonsenseQA extension

claims.claim: Finite-step failures, where a locally improving recurrent direction produces a harmful full update, occur in every model-task condition, including ones with positive mean gain.
claims.evidence_quote: Finite-step failures occur in all nine model–task conditions, including those with positive mean gain.

claims.claim: Applying only a quarter of the proposed update restores positive reference utility for most selected failures.
claims.evidence_quote: A fixed quarter step recovers positive gains in reference utility for 72.2–83.2% of selected failures across four settings.

claims.claim: Curvature-informed (quadratic) step selection recovers more failures than the fixed quarter step.
claims.evidence_quote: On Ouro-1.4B/GSM8K test at 4 → 5, it recovers 94.2% of the 431 finite-step failures, compared with 71.0% for the quarter step.

numbers.what: Mean scale prediction error (Ouro-1.4B/MATH-500, Huginn/GSM8K)
numbers.quote: Mean scale error is below 0.019 across 269 Ouro-1.4B/MATH-500 cases and 0.018 across 36 Huginn/GSM8K cases (Table 10).

numbers.what: Quadratic-rule recovery on Ouro-2.6B/HellaSwag across transitions 1->2 to 4->5
numbers.quote: on Ouro-2.6B/HellaSwag, where the quadratic rule recovers 88.0–100% of finite-step failures across four separately evaluated transitions from 1 → 2 through 4 → 5

limitations: Frozen models, single recurrent updates under teacher forcing; interventions evaluated before further recurrence, not during generation; accumulation of losses over trajectories not established; no curvature bound for Huginn's readout.
survey_notes: Mechanism for 'overthinking' in looped LMs: decline after an extra loop can reflect excessive displacement along a useful direction, motivating damping/step-size control (cf. residual damping, gating). Complements 2604.11791 (Ouro lacks fixed points) and 2609.21383 (prediction dynamics). Teacher-forced utility only; no end-to-end accuracy gain shown during generation.

title: Shared Weights, Selected Computations: How Looped Transformers Route What Each Loop Does
relevance_reason: Mechanistic study of what each loop computes, steering of frozen loops via the entering hidden state, and attention routing as the causal pathway (graph walks and Ouro-2.6B).
one_sentence: Shows that loops of a looped transformer do not follow a fixed one-loop-one-step rule; a learned linear map on the entering hidden state steers a frozen loop to different transitions, and attention-pattern patching shows routing carries this choice, including in Ouro-2.6B.
key_contributions: Intermediate decoded readouts on graph walks advance by varying numbers of steps per loop or stay at the target.
A linear map J at the loop boundary selects one-hop vs two-hop transitions of a frozen loop (48.2% to 99.6% one-hop accuracy).
Attention-pattern patching recovers steering effects and switches the semantic target (graph models and Ouro-2.6B); backbone supervision determines which transitions are steerable.

setup.model_sizes: Small graph-walk looped transformers (e.g. D8L6); Ouro-2.6B lightly fine-tuned on a letter-transfer task
setup.train_tokens_or_data: Synthetic graph walks, parity; Ouro fine-tuned on 1-4-step transfer requests
setup.loops_test: Ouro map applied before loops 2-4; graph models up to 16+ loops
setup.baselines: Unsteered frozen models; final-only vs stepwise supervised backbones (five matched pairs)
setup.benchmarks: Graph walk accuracy, multi-hop letter-transfer task, antonym cancellation, parity

claims.claim: Native recurrent trajectories need not follow one loop per algorithmic step: decoded predictions advance by different numbers of graph steps or stay at the reached target.
claims.evidence_quote: In the model's native trajectories, decoded predictions can advance by different numbers of graph steps or remain at a reached target, showing that recurrent progress need not follow a fixed one-loop-one-step pattern.

claims.claim: Changing only the hidden state entering a frozen loop via a learned linear map selects the next transition.
claims.evidence_quote: Without steering, one-hop accuracy is 48.2%, but with Jone it rises to 99.6%. Two-hop accuracy reaches 98.2% with Jtwo .

claims.claim: Patching attention patterns from steered runs transfers the steering effect, in graph models and in Ouro-2.6B.
claims.evidence_quote: In Ouro, steered patterns produce 248/256 correct answers, close to 251/256 under full steering.

claims.claim: Which transitions can be steered depends on backbone supervision, suggesting steering selects learned computations rather than creating new ones.
claims.evidence_quote: Across five matched pairs of graph models, changing intermediate supervision during backbone training changes which transitions J can induce.

numbers.what: Pattern vs output patch outcomes (D8L6 / Ouro)
numbers.quote: Pattern patches produce E in 77.8% of D8L6 cases and 71.1% of Ouro cases; output patches produce D in 80.9% and 93.8%, respectively.

numbers.what: Composition of one-hop map twice
numbers.quote: Applying the one-hop map twice reaches the two-hop target in 93.6% of examples. Omitting the second map reduces accuracy to 48.3%.

numbers.what: Graph continuation beyond map-training range
numbers.quote: On an independent held-out cycle subset, accuracy falls from 97.42% at loops 9–16 to 35.11% at loops

limitations: Mostly small synthetic graph models; Ouro experiment uses a lightly fine-tuned model on a constructed language task with selected heads; composed controllers are order-dependent and degrade with longer compositions; steering does not extrapolate beyond map-training depth.
survey_notes: Directly answers 'how loops route computation': the shared block acts as an executor routed by the entering state through attention patterns. Complements 2604.11791 (attention patterns freeze per layer at fixed points): here attention patterns are the steerable control channel. Relevance to safety: a small linear map at the loop boundary can redirect latent multi-step computation of a frozen model, a potential steering/control handle (and an attack surface), though the paper does not frame it as safety.

title: Looped Transformers under the Jacobian Lens: Does the Global Workspace Survive Recurrence?
relevance_reason: Applies Jacobian-lens readout and eleven causal intervention families to Ouro-2.6B and Huginn-0125 across loops; directly about decodability, steerability and verbalisation of latent content.
one_sentence: Extends the Jacobian lens to looped models via virtual unrolling and finds a verbalisable, steerable 'workspace' in Ouro-2.6B and Huginn-0125, but recurrence reshapes access: Ouro re-derives content every loop, Huginn carries it across 16 recurrences with only a ~2-recurrence transport horizon.
key_contributions: Virtual-unrolling adapter giving per-virtual-layer Jacobian lenses for weight-tied models, plus validation for recurrence-specific failure modes.
Transport structure: linear transport fails at Ouro's deep-supervised loop boundaries; Huginn's horizon is ~2 recurrences and its lenses repeat across iterations (cosine 0.9991).

Causal suite (writes, ablations, verbal report, introspection): Huginn reports swapped self-computed content 98% but never verbalises injected concepts (0/97); only deep-supervised Ouro reports injected concepts (top-1 31%).

setup.model_sizes: Ouro-2.6B (48 layers x 4, virtual depth 192), Huginn-0125 3.5B (2+4+2, core x16, virtual depth 68), Qwen3.6-27B baseline (64 untied layers); also Ouro-2.6B-Thinking
setup.loops_test: Ouro 4 loops; Huginn r=16
setup.baselines: Qwen3.6-27B under same harness
setup.benchmarks: Workspace suite of Gurnee et al. (lens readout, eleven causal experiment families)

claims.claim: A workspace (verbalisable, causally potent mid-depth content) forms in the iterated part of both looped models, but recurrence changes how it can be accessed.
claims.regime: unmatched (one checkpoint per family; architecture confounded with recipe and scale)
claims.evidence_quote: We find that a workspace forms in the iterated part of each architecture, but that recurrence changes how it can be accessed.

claims.claim: Ouro reconstructs workspace content each loop, so interventions must span all remaining loops; Huginn carries content across all recurrences but reads/writes act within a ~2-recurrence window.
claims.evidence_quote: Ouro reconstructs workspace content in every loop, and linear transport cannot carry that content across loop boundaries; writes and ablations must therefore span every remaining loop.

claims.claim: Verbalising newly injected content tracks explicit per-iteration (deep) supervision; Huginn never verbalises injected concepts, Ouro does at 31% top-1, and untied 27B Qwen is null.
claims.evidence_quote: Ouro, the one model trained that way, is the only one that reports an injected concept (top-1 31%); Huginn never does (0/97), and the 27B Qwen model shows that untied scale cannot substitute for this supervision.

claims.claim: In Huginn, content computed early stays present but unverbalised through later recurrences; this persistence is recomputation from the re-injected input, not a memory buffer.
claims.evidence_quote: content computed by recurrence 2–3 remains present, unverbalised, through every later recurrence. The analogy has a sharp limit — the injection-path experiments show this persistence is continuous recomputation from a re-injected input encoding, not a memory buffer;

claims.claim: The Jacobian lens is structurally blind to content not driving the current next token, so it cannot distinguish 'not held' from 'held but idle'.
claims.evidence_quote: The instrument therefore cannot distinguish "not held" from "held but idle"; the limitation is the same for all three models,

numbers.what: Huginn verbal report of swapped self-computed concept (top-5)
numbers.quote: swap a concept the model has already computed and is about to emit, and it reports the injected concept in its top-5 at 98% (124/126)

numbers.what: Ouro writes spanning all loops vs one loop
numbers.quote: forces any write to be maintained across every remaining loop's re-derivation (38% spanning all loops vs. 21% for one).

numbers.what: Agreement of independently fitted Huginn lenses at matched offsets
numbers.quote: independently fitted Huginn lenses at matched offsets agree at cosine 0.9991 — so one iteration's lens transfers to all

numbers.what: Ouro-2.6B-Thinking SFT size used for robustness check
numbers.quote: on Ouro-2.6B-Thinking, the reasoning SFT of our base checkpoint (∼8.3M supervised examples) shows that they are not.

limitations: Mean-Jacobian lenses are linearised, single-token-concept instruments that fail beyond their validated horizon and cannot see content not driving the next token; estimator-dependent readouts; one checkpoint per family confounds architecture with recipe and scale; no sweep over Huginn recurrence count.
builds_on: Gurnee et al. 2026 (Jacobian lens / global workspace)
survey_notes: Strongest LLM-scale evidence on decodability/steerability of intermediate loops. Safety-relevant: (i) Huginn holds computed content unverbalised across recurrences; (ii) the lens, a candidate latent monitor, is blind to idle content and invalid beyond its horizon, so absence of a readout is not evidence of absence; (iii) deep supervision (Ouro) makes loop boundaries token-aligned and more legible. Agrees with 2604.11791 that Ouro and Huginn differ sharply at loop boundaries (Ouro no fixed point vs Huginn fixed point). Contrasts with 2507.02199 which found Huginn's latent CoT hard to decode with logit lens; here a fitted lens decodes it within its horizon.

title: Dynamical phase selection controls compute scaling in looped transformers
relevance_reason: Dynamical-systems analysis of fixed points and bifurcations of a trained weight-tied block, linking phase to test-time iteration count.
one_sentence: Tiny looped transformers trained to identical accuracy on a decision task realize distinct dynamical phases (saddle-node fold, Neimark-Sacker, rigid) selected mainly by initialization, and the phase sets how inference time scales; fold phase gives a parameter-free law and N^-2 tail.
key_contributions: Classifies trained weight-tied maps into fold, Neimark-Sacker, rigid and monostable phases via continued Jacobian spectra; phase depends on initialization, not task accuracy.
Center-manifold normal form for the fold phase predicts relaxation time and spectral gap with the parameter-free relation tau(eps)[1-lambda_max(-eps)] -> pi, verified within a few percent.
Workload-level tail P(tau > N) ~ N^-2 for smooth difficulty densities; this law vanishes in the Neimark-Sacker phase.

setup.model_sizes: Latent dimension d=16-20, K=24 or 48 (tiny weight-tied pre-norm attention+MLP block)
setup.train_tokens_or_data: Synthetic sign(h) decision task with evidence withdrawn mid-episode in a fraction mu of trials
setup.loops_test: Iterated to convergence; relaxation time measured
setup.benchmarks: Held-out accuracy (all 1.000); relaxation-time distributions over 8.4e4 problems

claims.claim: Networks with identical architecture, objective and accuracy realize different dynamical phases depending on initialization, and the phase determines how test-time compute scales.
claims.evidence_quote: networks with identical architecture and objective, trained to identical accuracy, nevertheless realize distinct dynamical phases depending strongly on initialization, and that the bifurcation defining each phase determines how test-time compute scales.

claims.claim: Phase is identifiable early in training and does not switch between fold and Neimark-Sacker later.
claims.evidence_quote: eight of ten networks are already in their final phase by step 250; one additional network subsequently changes locally from a non-generic crossing to Neimark– Sacker, while none switches directly between fold and Neimark–Sacker,

claims.claim: In the fold phase, the distribution of required iterations has a heavy N^-2 tail, so rare hard instances dominate compute variance.
claims.evidence_quote: At N = 10N ∗ , the predicted unsolved fraction 10−2 is measured as 0.0070–0.0110 [Fig. 2(c)].

numbers.what: Phases at mu=0.50 across ten initializations
numbers.quote: At fixed µ = 0.50, ten independent initializations yield five folds, one Neimark–Sacker, one rigid, and three monostable networks, all with accuracy 1.000

numbers.what: Measured Pi at eps=1e-6 vs predicted pi
numbers.quote: Π at ε = 10−6 tail exponent, least squares tail exponent, Hill π = 3.1416 −2 2 3.146 ± 0.017

limitations: Toy dimension (d=16-20), single synthetic decision task; classification of observed bifurcations is not an exclusion theorem; no language-model experiments.
survey_notes: Theory-flavoured mechanism result: fixed-point structure and bifurcations of the trained map, not architecture, determine compute scaling and whether a convergence-based halting criterion is well behaved (Neimark-Sacker phase yields bounded non-stationary orbits, analogous to the 'orbits' in Huginn noted by 2604.11791). Synthetic only; extrapolation to LLMs is speculative.

title: Are Your Reasoning Models Reasoning or Guessing? A Mechanistic Analysis of Hierarchical Reasoning Models
relevance_reason: Mechanistic analysis of HRM's recurrent latent trajectories: fixed-point violations, grokking-like jumps across segments, multiple attractors.
one_sentence: Finds HRM violates its assumed fixed-point property (fails one-cell Sudokus), shows abrupt grokking-like error drops across segments and multiple (false) attractors, interprets recursion as guessing, and scales guesses to lift Sudoku-Extreme accuracy from 55.0% to 96.9%.
key_contributions: Fixed-point violation: HRM corrupts already-correct answers on trivially easy puzzles; data augmentation restores stability.
Per-sample trajectories show a long plateau then a sudden drop to zero error; latent trajectories reveal multiple fixed points and false attractors.
Guess-scaling strategies (data mixing, input relabeling perturbation, checkpoint bootstrapping) combined into Augmented HRM.

setup.loops_train: HRM segments (outer recursive loop) with one-step gradient
setup.loops_test: HRM segments
setup.baselines: Vanilla HRM
setup.benchmarks: Sudoku-Extreme

claims.claim: HRM's fixed-point property fails in practice: it often corrupts answers it already reached on very easy puzzles.
claims.evidence_quote: HRM frequently corrupts its answer by making unnecessary updates to its latent state, even after having reached the correct answer at very early segments (Figure 2.b).

claims.claim: Error does not fall gradually across segments; it plateaus and then drops suddenly, so segments are not incremental refinement steps.
claims.evidence_quote: After being quickly reduced to a relatively low value, the loss enters a lengthy plateau before suddenly dropping to zero.

claims.claim: Scaling the number and quality of 'guesses' (no extra parameters per model, ensemble over checkpoints) raises Sudoku-Extreme exact accuracy from 55.0% to 96.9%.
claims.regime: iso_param per model (bootstrapping uses an ensemble of 10 checkpoints)
claims.evidence_quote: Combining all methods, our Augmented HRM is able to boost the accuracy from 55.0% to 96.9% for Sudoku-Extreme,

numbers.what: HRM stability on one-cell/one-row puzzles
numbers.quote: In fact, HRM is only able to maintain stability on such puzzles about 75% of the time.

numbers.what: Gain from checkpoint bootstrapping
numbers.quote: However, we do observe a 9.2% improvement in accuracy with this model bootstrapping method.

limitations: Single task focus (Sudoku-Extreme); HRM inner H/L structure abstracted away; improvements rely on ensembling and perturbation, increasing compute; no language-model analysis.
survey_notes: Fixed-point evidence contrasts with 2604.11791's LLM finding that most tokens reach fixed points: in HRM, fixed points are violated and false attractors exist. Grokking-like jumps across recursions contradict a 'gradual refinement' reading of loops (cf. 2609.39892, non-uniform progress per loop). Consistent with 2609.22197 that HRM is a constraint-refinement/guessing system without clean stepwise reasoning.

title: Block-Recurrent Dynamics in Vision Transformers
relevance_reason: Shows dense ViTs can be rewritten as a few weight-tied blocks applied recurrently (Raptor) and analyzes depth as a dynamical system; vision, post-hoc recurrent surrogate rather than a natively looped LM.
one_sentence: Proposes the Block-Recurrent Hypothesis that trained ViTs' L layers can be rewritten as k<<L weight-tied blocks applied recurrently, verified by distilled Raptor surrogates (96% of DINOv2 linear-probe accuracy with 2 blocks), and studies the resulting depth dynamics.
key_contributions: Layer-layer similarity matrices across ViTs show contiguous phases; a max-cut algorithm finds phase boundaries; stochastic depth strengthens block recurrence.
Raptor: weight-tied block-recurrent surrogates trained to reproduce the teacher's full activation trajectory (teacher forcing then autoregressive).
Dynamical interpretability: class-dependent angular basins with self-correction, token-specific dynamics, low-rank late updates consistent with low-dimensional attractors.

setup.model_sizes: Small-scale ViTs; DINOv2 foundation model (teacher)
setup.loops_train: k=2 or 3 recurrent blocks matching teacher depth
setup.loops_test: Same as training
setup.baselines: Teacher ViT (DINOv2)
setup.benchmarks: ImageNet-1k linear probe accuracy (DINOv2); CIFAR-100 for small ViTs; layerwise representational R^2
